title: Ten Indians and Indian-Origin Leaders Named to TIME100 AI 2026 List
excerpt: From Sarvam AI's foundational models to IBM's enterprise strategy, Indian names span all four categories of TIME's annual ranking of the most influential people in artificial intelligence.
body:
• Ten Indians and Indian-origin professionals feature on TIME's 2026 list of the 100 most influential people in AI, published on August 27
  • The honorees span corporate leadership, foundational AI research, healthcare, semiconductors, AI governance, and legal accountability
  • IBM CEO Arvind Krishna is among 17 names on TIME's worldwide cover, listed under the Leaders category
  • India-based honorees include Sarvam AI co-founder Vivek Raghavan and Adalat AI's Utkarsh Saxena, reflecting the country's growing domestic AI ecosystem

TIME published the fourth edition of its TIME100 AI list on August 27, naming 100 people across four categories — Leaders, Innovators, Shapers, and Thinkers — who are shaping the development and deployment of artificial intelligence. Ten Indians and people of Indian origin made the cut, their work spanning foundational AI models, enterprise technology, semiconductors, healthcare, and governance.

Corporate and Government Leaders

Arvind Krishna, Chairman and CEO of IBM, appears under Leaders and is one of 17 listmakers featured on TIME's worldwide cover. Born in Andhra Pradesh and an IIT Kanpur graduate, Krishna has led IBM since 2020. He has advocated for smaller, more efficient AI models designed for specific business tasks, while keeping IBM open to larger systems from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic when customers need them.

Arvind Raman, Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology and acting head of the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is also listed under Leaders. He oversees work that tests the capabilities and potential risks of advanced AI models, with findings shared across the US government.

The Innovators

Vivek Raghavan, co-founder of Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI, is listed under Innovators for his work on AI sovereignty. Raghavan spent over a decade working on Aadhaar before co-founding Sarvam in 2023 with Pratyush Kumar. The company released its 30-billion and 105-billion parameter open-weight models in March and introduced Sarvam Vision, a vision-language model covering 22 Indian languages. In August, Nvidia joined an extension that completed Sarvam's $300 million Series B, valuing the company at approximately $1.5 billion.

"Indians are exporting data and importing intelligence — a trade he compares to the country exporting cotton and importing cloth a century ago."

— TIME's profile of Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam AI

Utkarsh Saxena, co-founder and CEO of Adalat AI, also appears under Innovators. Adalat AI builds speech and language tools for Indian courtrooms, working to reduce transcription and case-management bottlenecks that slow the judicial system.

Anima Anandkumar, Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences at Caltech and an IIT Madras alumna, is recognized for AI-based methods that model physical processes at speeds more than a million times those of earlier approaches. Her applications range from weather forecasting to quantum computing and nuclear-fusion simulations. She joined the UN Secretary-General's Scientific Advisory Board in March.

Suchi Saria, founder and CEO of Bayesian Health, made the list for applying machine learning to clinical decision-making. Her system received FDA clearance in May for continuous AI monitoring that alerts clinicians when patients may be at risk of sepsis.

Sanjay Mehrotra, Chairman, President, and CEO of Micron Technology, is recognized under Innovators. Micron is one of only three companies worldwide manufacturing high-bandwidth memory, a critical component used alongside advanced AI chips.

Shapers and Thinkers

Sunny Gandhi, 24, co-executive director of Encode, appears under Shapers. The youth-led organization works on AI policy and advocacy in the United States. Gandhi helped advance California's SB 1047 AI safety bill through the state legislature in 2024, although Governor Gavin Newsom later vetoed the measure.

Meetali Jain, founder and executive director of Tech Justice Law, is under Shapers for her work on legal accountability in AI. Her organization's first major case involved the family of Sewell Setzer III, a teenager who died by suicide in 2024 after allegedly interacting with a Character.AI chatbot. Character.AI and Google later settled the case.

Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant, rounds out the Indian-origin contingent under the Thinkers category. The former nuclear scientist has argued that artificial intelligence could challenge traditional assumptions about the link between capital investment and employment.

Across the AI Stack

The ten names span a wide cross-section of the AI economy. Raghavan and Saxena are building from India, developing products tailored to the country's linguistic and institutional needs. Krishna, Mehrotra, and Ravi Kumar lead global corporations that are deploying AI at enterprise scale. Anandkumar and Saria represent research and healthcare applications. Raman, Gandhi, and Jain are working on how AI should be governed, tested, and held accountable.

The list underscores the growing Indian imprint on global AI — not just in corporate boardrooms, but in the research labs, courtrooms, and regulatory offices where the technology's future is being shaped.
